title: Training Language Models to Fail Gracefully

paper.title: Training Language Models to Fail Gracefully Thanks: Project website, code, and other assets: https://zanette-labs.github.io/failing-gracefully/
paper.abstract: Abstract Reinforcement learning makes language models better at solving tasks, but the same mechanism also rewards guessing. When success is the only way to earn reward, opting for a safe fallback is always worse than a long-shot attempt. When a wrong action can corrupt a database or ship broken code, that incentive can be costly. Therefore, we propose training models to fail gracefully : to preserve successful behavior whenever possible while learning to execute a safe fallback policy when acting would be unreliable. However, naively using policy gradients with intermediate reward for fallback behavior is brittle due to unfavorable optimization dynamics. We address this challenge with GracefulRL , which reshapes the optimization landscape to promote graceful failure. Importantly, this behavior emerges directly from outcome-level reward signals, without annotations specifying when to fall back or additional inference-time machinery such as a verifier. Across a range of tasks and scales, we train models that largely preserve their task-solving capability while selectively falling back when acting would be unreliable. More broadly, our results show that reinforcement learning can not only incentivize models to succeed, but also to reason about the limits of their capabilities and change course when they determine that success is out of reach.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Large Language Models (LLMs) can now complete in minutes tasks that would take a person hours. They write and refactor code across whole repositories, produce long mathematical arguments, and act as agents that edit files and run commands on our behalf. Significant improvements in such capabilities can be attributed to Reinforcement learning (RL) in domains with verifiable rewards such as coding and mathematics, ( Guo et al., 2025 ; OpenAI et al., 2026 ; Shao et al., 2024 ) where models are rewarded for successful task completion ( Lambert et al., 2025 ; Luo et al., 2025 ) . These improvements are often measured by metrics such as accuracy or success rate, but these metrics say little about how the model behaves when it does not succeed . Models are imperfectly informed and computationally bounded during inference. Therefore, there always exist situations in which appropriate actions cannot be reliably determined. In such cases, reinforcement learning can incentivize guessing, as a strategy to maximize reward ( Kalai et al., 2025 ) , laying the burden of verification on the user. Someone needs to check the proof, review the pull request, and confirm what the agent actually did. This verification can be tedious and prone to errors, and when it fails, mistakes can propagate into consequential actions. Therefore, we want models that change course when success is unlikely. If they can solve a task reliably, they should. If they cannot, they should do something else: revert their changes, inform the user that they are stuck, or hand the task to a different model. We call this behaviour failing gracefully . Not only does graceful failure avoid harmful actions, it also helps build trust with users. The naive way to train for this behavior is to reward success most, fallback second, and failure least. In principle, this should teach the model to keep trying when success is within reach and to fallback when it is not. Surprisingly, we find that learning this behavior with standard policy-gradient methods ( Williams, 1992 ) and their derivatives ( Shao et al., 2024 ) can be brittle. In the worst case, they can collapse to a model that always falls back and stops solving the task altogether (Section 3 ). We trace this failure to unfavorable optimization dynamics : the objective expresses the behavior we want, but the optimization process does not reliably produce it. We introduce GracefulRL , a reinforcement learning approach designed to avoid this pathology. We modify the optimization landscape which lets us maintain pressure to solve the task, while simultaneously encouraging the model to fall back rather than making an error when success is unlikely. Crucially, the model learns when to fall back from its own interaction with the environment with no labels specifying which problems are too hard, and no separate uncertainty model or post-hoc decision rule at inference time. Across navigation, mathematical reasoning, and multi-turn Minesweeper, GracefulRL learns selective fallback while preserving strong task performance. On AIME, it reduces the error rate from 79.1% to 8.9% while sacrificing only 3.1 percentage points of success relative to standard RL. In Minesweeper, it improves both sides of the tradeoff, increasing success while reducing errors. Perhaps most strikingly, we find that the model verbalizes its decision making strategy in its chain-of-thought when its about to change course. Overall, our results suggest that reinforcement learning can not only improve a model’s task performance, but also shape it’s behavior when success is unlikely. Figure 1: Learning to fail gracefully. (a) GracefulRL augments standard RLVR with an explicit fallback behavior, ordered as Success ≻ Fallback ≻ Error \textsc{Success}\succ\textsc{Fallback}\succ\textsc{Error} . (b) Standard policy gradient (PG) can lose optimization signal near saturated policies. In contrast, the GracefulRL objective retains a non-vanishing gradient. (c) Using models trained with GracefulRL on the AIME benchmark, the most cautious model ( c = 0.8 c=0.8 ) reduces the error rate from 79.1 % 79.1\% to 8.9 % 8.9\% , an 88.8 % 88.8\% relative reduction, while success only drops by 3.1% compared to RL with binary rewards ( c = 0 c=0 ).

sections.heading: 3 The Challenge of Optimizing Fallback Behavior
sections.text: A natural approach is to use the ternary reward in Section 2 in a policy-gradient algorithm which maximizes the expected reward, that is maximize 𝒥 PG ​ ( x ) = p S ​ ( x ) + c ​ p F ​ ( x ) . \mathcal{J}_{\mathrm{PG}}(x)=p_{S}(x)+c\,p_{F}(x). Unfortunately, we find that this approach is highly sensitive to initialization and reward magnitude, necessitating tuning for every model and task combination. In the worst case, the policy can converge to a degenerate one that always executes the fallback with no task progress, or doesn’t learn to fallback at all. Vanishing gradients near saturated policies. Why does such a natural objective exhibit this behavior? Formally, we show that this pathology emerges because the policy gradient vanishes when the policy approaches saturation. This implies that if the policy saturated on suboptimal outcomes during training, it can lead to poor convergence. We make a formal claim. Proposition 1: Gradient suppression near saturated policies [ Proof: App. A ] Under the regularity conditions mentioned in Appendix A , for all possible outcomes of the policy o ∈ { Success , Fallback , Error } o\in\{\textsc{Success},\textsc{Fallback},\textsc{Error}\} , p o → 1 ⇒ ‖ ∇ θ 𝒥 PG ​ ( x ) ‖ = O ⁡ ( 1 − p o ​ ( x ) ) . p_{o}\rightarrow 1\quad\Rightarrow\quad\left\|\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{J}_{\mathrm{PG}}(x)\right\|=O\!\left(1-p_{o}(x)\right). Intuitively, as the policy places nearly all of its probability on a single outcome, the gradient shrinks proportionally to the probability mass remaining on the other outcomes. Thus, once the policy becomes nearly deterministic, for example, always falling back, the gradient update required to move probability back toward success becomes vanishingly small. This result applies to standard softmax-parameterized policies, including auto-regressive language models, under a mild boundedness condition on the gradients of the logits. For a detailed exposition, refer to Appendix A .

sections.heading: 5 Experiments
sections.text: Motivated by our theoretical insights, we study GracefulRL in three practical settings. Our first setting involves a maze navigation task with a small ResNet ( He et al., 2016 ) policy. This gives us a compute-efficient setup that allows us to scale training steps and examine the effects of different hyperparameters. Next, we move to a relevant problem: training LLMs to abstain on mathematical reasoning problems. Here we test whether GracefulRL scales to more realistic scenarios and also test meaningful generalization across different domains. Finally, we design an experiment where an LLM has to make irreversible sequential decisions in the Minesweeper game, where we discover that training for graceful failure can sometimes improve task performance as well.

Environment. For our first experimental setting, we introduce SafeMaze , a maze navigation task where an agent can either reach the Goal , which counts as Success , or navigate to a designated Safe square, which counts as Fallback . Crucially, the Safe square is deliberately much easier to reach: it is connected to the start by an always-clear passage, whereas reaching the Goal requires solving the maze within 50 50 steps or less. The mazes are designed in a way that Goal is always reachable (see Figure 3 for an example). Hitting a wall or timing out counts as an Error . Thus, the agent faces exactly the tradeoff of interest: pursue the harder task for the possibility of success, or take an easy and reliable fallback that avoids error but forgoes success . We use a 4M parameter, slightly pre-trained residual CNN as the policy here. More details are given in Appendix C .

sections.heading: 5.1.1 Results on SafeMaze
sections.text: Standard policy gradient methods are brittle. First, we train GRPO and RLOO on the SafeMaze task with a fixed value of the reward for reaching Safe , set to 0.4. We observe that, neither of these variants learn a meaningful policy. Within a few gradient steps, the policy reaches a 100 % 100\% fallback rate and stops solving the task (Figure 3 ). In general, we observe that this behavior is highly sensitive to the fallback reward c c . In Appendix C.2 , using c = 0.1 c=0.1 for RLOO drives the fallback probability toward zero. At c = 0.2 c=0.2 , training retains some success but quickly plateaus. For every tested c ≥ 0.3 c\geq 0.3 , the policy rapidly collapses to the fallback-only solution. Thus, useful behavior only occurs in a narrow range of fallback rewards rather than emerging robustly from the desired reward ordering. Appendix C.6 shows that entropy bonuses also do not help in improving performance. Comparing with other baselines. Next, we compare with two stronger baselines. We observe that a meaningful policy can be learnt with RLOO when the reward for Safe is lower than the success rate of the policy. Motivated by this at time step t t , online reward tuning uses c = α ⋅ p ^ S , t c=\alpha\cdot\widehat{p}_{S,t} where p ^ S , t \widehat{p}_{S,t} denotes the online success rate. We also test Delightful Policy Gradient (DPG) ( Osband, 2026 ) that modifies policy-gradient updates to mitigate trapping near deterministic sub-optimal policies ( Mei and Osband, 2026 ) . Figure 3 shows the reliability curve for each method after 20 20 k training steps for different hyperparameters. We see a clear trend: GracefulRL converges to a higher Success ​ @ ⁡ 1 \operatorname{Success@}1 at lower Error ​ @ ⁡ 1 \operatorname{Error@}1 compared to the baselines. Thus, GracefulRL is robust to reward magnitudes unlike standard policy gradient and learns useful fallback behavior when uncertain. Finally, we also investigate the interplay of various hyperparameters, specifically the role of the number of rollouts N N , the fallback reward c c , and the smoothing parameter ϵ {\epsilon} in Appendix C.4 and Appendix C.5 . We observe that performance improves with more rollouts N N , particularly at higher values of c c , and also that a higher ϵ {\epsilon} value gives higher reward at smaller compute budgets.

sections.text: Figure 4: (a) Training for abstention using standard policy gradient (RLOO) can converge to a policy that always abstains, while our method learns a meaningful policy. (b), (c) Reliability frontiers for the trained Qwen3-1.7B-Base and Qwen3-4B-Base models, comparing RLCR+Thresholding and GracefulRL . GracefulRL achieves a higher success rate at a lower error rate. Another important instance of graceful failure is abstention . We study this setting in mathematical reasoning, our first LLM testbed. Here, a model must make two decisions: how to solve a problem, and whether it should attempt a final answer at all. For problems within its capabilities, the model should reason through them and produce a solution. For problems beyond its current competence, however, continuing to reason toward a final answer can lead to a confident but incorrect prediction. A graceful model should instead recognize when its reasoning is unlikely to succeed and abstain . We therefore ask whether outcome-level RL can teach a language model not only to solve problems, but also to recognize when to stop trying. We first describe the experimental setup and the baseline. RLCR+Thresholding baseline. We compare against Reinforcement Learning with Calibration Rewards (RLCR) ( Damani et al., 2026 ) , a recent uncertainty quantification approach, which trains language models for calibration. In RLCR, a model is trained to generate an answer and a confidence score q ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] q\in[0,1] , and is then trained using a Brier-score based reward, that is, for a response y y for prompt x x , r RLCR = 𝕀 correctness ​ ( y , x ) − ( 𝕀 correctness ​ ( y , x ) − q ) 2 r_{\mathrm{RLCR}}=\mathbb{I}_{\textrm{correctness}}(y,x)-\left(\mathbb{I}_{\textrm{correctness}}(y,x)-q\right)^{2} 1 1 1 We give a reward of − 1.1 -1.1 for malformed outputs, since − 1 -1 is the minimum value of r RLCR . r_{\textrm{RLCR}}. . To obtain a policy that abstains, we use a test time threshold τ \tau , where the model answers if confidence q ≥ τ q\geq\tau and abstains otherwise. Conditioned training (ours). For GracefulRL , we jointly train a single model across five fallback utilities c ∈ { 0 , 0.2 , 0.4 , 0.6 , 0.8 } c\in\{0,0.2,0.4,0.6,0.8\} . We append a conditioning suffix to each problem indicating the desired degree of caution. For c = 0 c=0 , it reads “Be very optimistic and always attempt an answer, even if you are unsure,” while for c = 0.8 c=0.8 it reads “Be quite careful and avoid guessing.” The complete set appears in Appendix Table 3 . During training, we mix examples from all five conditioning levels and optimize each using the corresponding value of c c , where correct answers, abstentions, and incorrect answers correspond to the Success , Fallback , and Error outcomes, respectively. Training and evaluation. We train the Qwen3-1.7B-Base and Qwen3-4B-Base ( Yang et al., 2025 ) models on the DAPO-Math-17K dataset ( Yu et al., 2025 ) using on-policy RL for 1,500 1{,}500 steps and 1,000 1{,}000 steps respectively. For evaluation, we use MATH500 ( Hendrycks et al., 2021 ) , AIME 2024-2026, AMC 2022-2024, and JEEBench (numeric) ( Arora et al., 2023 ) . At test time, for RLCR, we sweep the threshold τ \tau to trace its reliability curve, whereas for GracefulRL , we evaluate on each unique conditioning prompt, to measure the policy’s reliability. Details are given in Appendix D .

We evaluate our model trained on math problems on AbstentionBench ( Kirichenko et al., 2025 ) , which contains unknown, underspecified, and otherwise unanswerable questions from diverse domains such as History, MedicalQA, Geography and MoralQA. We find that the model retains its intended behavior. More cautious suffixes produce more fallbacks on questions that can’t be answered reliably, while optimistic suffixes attempt more responses. The average abstention F 1 F_{1} score rises from 0.472 0.472 at c = 0.2 c=0.2 to 0.677 0.677 at c = 0.8 c=0.8 outperforming the Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 model which scores 0.590 0.590 (Figure 6 ). This indicates hints of generalization to domains other than mathematical reasoning. Detailed results on the entire benchmark appear in Appendix D.10 .

sections.heading: 5.3 Multi-Turn RL in Minesweeper
sections.text: Finally, we use an LLM as an agent in a multi-turn Minesweeper game ( Tajwar et al., 2025 ) . This setting gives us a testbed that involves a sequential decision-making environment with irreversible actions. The environment consists of a grid containing hidden mines and revealed cells which indicate the number of mines in their neighboring cells. At each step, the agent observes the current board state and selects a cell to reveal. The game has N N turns and the rules are as follows: 1. Revealing a mine immediately ends the game with an Error . 2. Successfully revealing all non-mine cells by the end of the game, results in Success . 3. Avoiding mines but not revealing all non-mine squares by the end is a Fallback . The Fallback behavior promotes conservative actions, even if it means giving up on completing the puzzle. Minesweeper pushes graceful failure beyond one-shot uncertainty estimation. The agent must repeatedly decide whether the available evidence justifies another action, with every move changing both the available information and the uncertainty of subsequent decisions. Consequently, methods such as RLCR or majority-vote thresholding, which attach confidence to a single generated answer, do not directly apply in this scenario . This makes Minesweeper a natural setting for end-to-end policy optimization from outcome-level rewards . We examine whether GracefulRL can teach the agent when to keep playing and when continued action is no longer worth the risk . Training and Evaluation. We train Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 for 250 RL steps on puzzles requiring N = 8 N=8 steps to solve and evaluate on 500 500 held-out puzzles meant to be solved at a N = 12 N=12 -turn budget. Appendix E specifies the board construction, training configuration, and evaluation protocol.

sections.heading: 6 Related Work
sections.text: Policy-gradient optimization challenges. Vanishing gradients in policy gradients are well known, studied even in tabular MDPs ( Agarwal et al., 2021 ) . Mei et al. (2020) identify a “gravity well” induced by the softmax parameterization, leading to poor optimization while Li et al. (2021) further show that softmax PG methods can require exponentially many steps to converge. More recently, Razin et al. (2024) studied vanishing gradients in LLM RL finetuning showing that the gradient becomes small when the reward variance of the policy is small. Our analysis complements these results by studying a specific case with 3 outcomes where standard PG methods can get trapped near saturated outcomes. We further show that the GracefulRL objective avoids this pathology, retaining a non-vanishing optimization signal near such saturated solutions. Likelihood-based objectives for RL. Recent work has explored replacing expected-reward objectives with likelihood-based objectives exemplified by MaxRL ( Tajwar et al., 2026 ) and TailRL ( Ramasubramanian et al., 2026 ) . They show that these objectives admit an interpretation as a harmonically weighted combination of Best ​ @ ⁡ k \operatorname{Best@}k objectives. We arrive at the same solution through an optimization perspective. We analyse how the logarithmic objective avoids gradient suppression near undesirable saturation which prevents a failure mode in expected reward maximization. Uncertainty quantification for LLMs. Selective classification studies the tradeoff between prediction risk and coverage ( Chow, 1970 ; El-Yaniv and Wiener, 2010 ; Geifman and El-Yaniv, 2019 ; Liu et al., 2019 ) . Recent work on LLM uncertainty and abstention has constructed specialized data to train refusal behavior ( Zhang et al., 2024 ; Zhao et al., 2026 ) , elicited verbalized confidence ( Kadavath et al., 2022 ; Lin et al., 2022 ; Tian et al., 2023 ; Xiong et al., 2024 ) , estimated uncertainty through repeated sampling ( Manakul et al., 2023 ; Kang et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2023 ) , combined multiple models at inference time ( Stengel-Eskin et al., 2024 ) , directly trained models for uncertainty quantification ( Damani et al., 2026 ; Leng et al., 2025 ; Chandak et al., 2026 ) , or introduced inference-time stopping rules that detect when continued reasoning is unlikely to help ( Davidov et al., 2026 ) . Our goal however is different: rather than estimating uncertainty, we aim to learn how the policy should act under uncertainty . This distinction becomes important in sequential decision-making settings, where uncertainty quantification is not enough: the fallback policy execution must also be a part of the policy itself and its learnt end-to-end. Moreover, our approach doesn’t require specialized datasets, is not LLM-specific, and naturally extends to multi-step interactions. Learning abstention with RL. Some prior works try to use RL for abstention. For instance, Xu et al. (2024) use knowledge feedback to identify questions outside a model’s knowledge boundary and reward rejection on these examples. Wei et al. (2026) , Pan et al. (2026) , Ma et al. (2026) , Wu et al. (2026) and Zhai et al. (2026) directly train for abstention using policy gradient style methods such as GRPO and PPO with and without heuristics such as reward tuning or modifying advantages. However, we show that this procedure can be brittle depending on the model and the task. We show that our approach is more robust and avoids issues associated with PG methods in a principled manner. Moreover, our formulation treats fallback as a general behavior rather than an LLM-specific refusal, allowing it to extend to sequential and non-language decision-making settings. Safe and constrained reinforcement learning. Our work is also related to safe RL, which studies improving task performance while satisfying safety requirements or constraints ( García and Fernández, 2015 ; Achiam et al., 2017 ) . Other approaches intervene when an unsafe action is likely; for example, Recovery RL learns a separate recovery policy that takes control near constraint-violating regions ( Thananjeyan et al., 2021 ) . In contrast, we jointly learn task success and graceful fallback, without a secondary recovery policy intervening.

sections.heading: 7 Conclusion and Limitations
sections.text: We formulated graceful failure as an RL problem in which an agent must learn when to pursue task success and when to fall back safely. We showed that naively optimizing the expected reward can be brittle due to the underlying optimization dynamics. To address it, we introduced GracefulRL which provides a suitable landscape for optimization to succeed. Across the settings studied in this work, GracefulRL learns favorable tradeoffs between task success and error, demonstrating that fallback behavior can be learned directly as part of the policy. However, our method is designed for online RL, and we have not studied its behavior under off-policy training. We also do not investigate settings involving coding agents or long horizon agentic training due to constraints on compute. Finally, specifying appropriate fallback behavior can be difficult and may differ substantially across domains. Defining graceful failure across different domains, deriving scaling laws for it, and evaluating its generalization to unseen tasks remains an important direction for future research.

sections.heading: Appendix A Proof of the Results in Section 3
sections.text: 1. First, we fix terminology and show some simple identities which relate outcome probabilities to conditional score functions in Section A.1 . 2. Second, we show that under a boundedness assumption on the logit gradients, a standard regularity condition, the conditional score functions are bounded in Section A.2 . 3. Then, we show that this causes the gradient of the expected reward objective to vanish when the policy approaches saturation in Section A.3 , 4. Finally, we show that under a non-degeneracy condition, the gradient of the log-barrier based objective does not vanish near sub-optimal saturation in Section A.4 . It is worth noting that our proofs are only for the population level gradients and not for stochastic estimators which we leave for future work.

sections.text: For the SafeMaze environment, we generate a 15 × 15 15\times 15 grid and pretrain the policy using a mixture of Goal -seeking and Safe -square-seeking trajectories. We ensure that the Goal is always reachable in the grid within the time limit.

sections.heading: C.2 RLOO with a Fixed Fallback Reward
sections.text: Figure 8 shows why selecting a fixed reward for fallback when using policy gradient is difficult. With c = 0.1 c=0.1 , the fallback probability tends to zero, so the policy continues attempting the goal but incurs a high error rate. At c = 0.2 c=0.2 , close to the policy’s initial pass rate, RLOO retains nonzero success, but its performance plateaus while fallback remains the dominant outcome. For every tested reward c ≥ 0.3 c\geq 0.3 , the policy instead converges rapidly to the fallback-only solution, with p F → 1 p_{F}\to 1 and p S → 0 p_{S}\to 0 . Thus, a fixed reward gives useful behavior only in a narrow range and does not reliably support continued improvement. This motivates the online reward-tuning baseline, which sets the fallback reward relative to the policy’s current success rate rather than choosing a single value for the entire run. Figure 8: RLOO with fixed fallback rewards on SafeMaze. We measure p S , p F , p E p_{S},p_{F},p_{E} during training for c = 0.1 c=0.1 , c = 0.2 c=0.2 , and c ≥ 0.3 c\geq 0.3 . Empirically, we observe that when c ≪ p S c\ll p_{S} , the policy can lead to no coverage on fallback trajectories, that is, p F → 0 p_{F}\rightarrow 0 . Similarly, when c ≫ p S c\gg p_{S} , the policy can lead to a degenerate policy where it always goes to the Safe square.

sections.text: We jointly sweep the number of rollouts per update N ∈ { 16 , 32 , 64 } N\in\{16,32,64\} and the reward for reaching Safe , c ∈ { 0 , 0.2 , 0.4 , 0.6 , 0.8 } c\in\{0,0.2,0.4,0.6,0.8\} . Figure 9 (a) plots the resulting reliability frontiers after 5,000 5{,}000 training steps. We observe that increasing N N improves the reliability frontier. This can be explained by the fact that larger rollout counts provide a higher-order truncation of the log objective and are more likely to include rare successful trajectories, producing a more informative update. The effect of rollout count becomes more pronounced as the fallback reward increases. At c = 0.8 c=0.8 , the 16 16 - and 32 32 -rollout runs collapse to the fallback-only solution, whereas 64 64 rollouts retain nonzero success. Thus, settings that place greater value on reliability also require more rollouts to approximate a higher order approximation of the objective.

sections.text: As discussed in Section B , ϵ {\epsilon} smoothing can lower variance at the cost of some bias. sections.heading: C.6 Entropy-Bonus Tuning
sections.text: We also sweep the entropy-bonus strength for GRPO and RLOO while fixing the safe reward to c = 0.4 c=0.4 and holding everything else fixed. Entropy regularization does not yield a meaningful policy in this regime. Figure 10 shows that every setting drives p S p_{S} to zero within a few optimization steps. GRPO converges to the fallback-only policy across the entire sweep. RLOO does the same for entropy coefficients up to 0.3 0.3 , while the largest coefficient, 1 1 , instead converges to p E = 1 p_{E}=1 . sections.heading: D.5 RLCR Can Trade Accuracy for Calibration
sections.text: Figure 15: Training dynamics of the Qwen3-4B-Base RLCR policy on AIME. Although the Brier score generally improves (decreases) throughout training, answer accuracy peaks early and then declines. The RLCR reward combines these two quantities and therefore need not track accuracy. Figure 15 reveals that optimizing RLCR can trade task accuracy for improved calibration: after accuracy peaks around step 400 400 , the Brier score continues to improve while accuracy falls. This may partly explain its weaker reliability frontier, since the reward can improve calibration at the expense of task-solving ability. We hypothesize that optimizing calibration with methods such as TailRL could preserve more accuracy, and leave for future work. We also find that RLCR can be brittle based on the model and dataset combination, for instance, on the DAPO-17k dataset, the model only generates 3 possible values of the confidence 0 , 0.1 0,0.1 and 0.2 0.2 . However, this problem is not present in the 4B model.

It uses the same five conditioning suffixes as GracefulRL , but trains with RLOO and adapts the fallback reward to the policy’s observed success rate. A correct answer receives reward 1 1 , an incorrect answer receives 0 0 , and a fallback receives α ​ p ^ S , c , t \alpha\widehat{p}_{S,c,t} with α = c \alpha=c . Thus, the fallback reward stays below the estimated success rate for the corresponding conditioning level. The remaining training setup follows the conditioned-model runs described in Appendix D.1 . For Qwen3-1.7B-Base, fallback falls below 0.5 % 0.5\% around step 260 260 and remains negligible for the rest of the 1,500 1{,}500 -step run. For Qwen3-4B-Base, fallback initially rises to roughly 30 % 30\% , but after sustained training it abruptly collapses below 0.5 % 0.5\% around step 850 850 . Over the last 50 50 steps, the 4B model falls back on fewer than 0.1 % 0.1\% of training rollouts, while its failure rate reaches about 57 % 57\% . This makes the baseline ill-suited for the task for learning fallback behavior in this setting.

sections.heading: D.10 Evaluation on AbstentionBench
sections.text: We evaluate on AbstentionBench ( Kirichenko et al., 2025 ) , a benchmark assembled specifically to test whether a model declines to answer when a question cannot be answered as it is posed. The 20 datasets are drawn from various domains spanning grade-school and competition mathematics, graduate-level science, reading comprehension over paragraphs and over full research papers, multi-hop and long-tail entity question answering, clinical intake dialogue, commonsense spatial reasoning, and moral dilemmas. They also span six qualitatively different reasons for which a question may be unanswerable: an underspecified context that omits a premise the question depends on (thirteen partitions, e.g. GSM8K , SQuAD 2.0 , MMLU , GPQA ), an answer that is not known to anyone at present ( BB/Known-Unknowns , CoCoNot/Unknowns ), a false premise embedded in the question ( FalseQA , QAQA , KUQ/False-assumptions ), an inherently subjective question ( MoralChoice , CoCoNot/Subjective ), an underspecified intent that admits several readings ( SituatedQA , KUQ/Ambiguous ), and stale questions whose answer has changed since training ( CoCoNot/Temporal ). Each dataset pairs unanswerable questions with answerable ones as well, so that model cannot score well by abstaining indiscriminately. Figure 19: Per-dataset abstention performance on AbstentionBench . Abstention F 1 F_{1} across twenty datasets for GracefulRL at c ∈ { 0.2 , 0.4 , 0.6 , 0.8 } c\in\{0.2,0.4,0.6,0.8\} (orange) and Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 (blue). The methods use matching per-dataset sample counts and class balance; the effect of conditioning varies by dataset. Sampling. Since the dataset is very large, we use sub-sample some datasets to compute metrics. For the three datasets that ship an official 3,500 3{,}500 -example subsample ( BBQ , SQuAD 2.0 , ALCUNA ) we apply it first, so that our pool matches the one used in the original release. From each dataset we then draw at most 500 500 examples by stratified sampling on the should_abstain label, which reproduces the dataset’s own class ratio to within 0.2 0.2 percentage points; five datasets are smaller than 500 500 and are evaluated in full ( BB/Known-Unknowns , 46 46 ; MMLU-History , 78 78 ; GPQA , 80 80 ; BB/Disambiguate , 250 250 ; MMLU-Math , 266 266 ). This yields 8,220 8{,}220 prompts per condition, of which 3,678 3{,}678 ( 44.7 % 44.7\% ) are unanswerable. Inference details. For GracefulRL , every prompt uses the training-time instruction format verbatim, differing only in the one-sentence risk cue that encodes the abstention reward c c ; we sweep c ∈ { 0.2 , 0.4 , 0.6 , 0.8 } c\in\{0.2,0.4,0.6,0.8\} , the range seen during training. We decode 1 response per prompt with temperature 0.6 0.6 , top- p p 0.95 0.95 , a 4,096 4{,}096 -token generation budget and a 32,768 32{,}768 -token context (long enough for QASPER , whose longest prompt is ≈ 30 \approx\!30 k tokens), giving 32,880 32{,}880 generations in total. Evaluation. Since GracefulRL is trained to signal abstention with a literal \boxed{\text{I don’t know}} , its abstention is detected by exact match, removing the need for an LLM-as-a-judge as done in the original evaluation by the authors. For the Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 model, however, we use the author’s evaluation pipeline. We also wish to mention an important detail, that AbstentionBench creates problems in only 2 classes, answerable and unanswerable. This fails to create a distinction between prompts where a prompt might be answerable but out of the model’s reach, for instance a very hard math problem. Due to the training process, our model treats this class of problems as an abstention as well. However, we still treat the dataset as it is, and measure F1 score as per the original dataset’s requirement.

sections.heading: E.1 Game, observations, and outcomes
sections.text: Each puzzle is a 6 × 6 6\times 6 Minesweeper board with six mines and 30 safe cells. Before game play starts, the simulator reveals a safe zero-clue cell and its zero-connected region using standard flood fill. The model then receives the visible board as a Python list, with hidden cells shown as # and opened cells as integer counts of adjacent mines. The only action available to the model is reveal(row, col) . Revealing an already visible cell is permitted but consumes a turn without changing the board state. An episode is a Success when all 30 safe cells are visible. Revealing a mine, unparseable action, or out-of-bounds action terminates the episode with an Error . Reaching the turn limit without solving or making one of these terminal errors is counted as a Fallback . Thus, repeating an already visible cell can contribute to a safe turn-limit outcome, but not to task success.

sections.heading: E.2 Puzzle generation and data splits
sections.text: • A puzzle is initialized by a random seed. For each generation attempt, the generator chooses an opening cell, excludes that cell and its eight neighbors from mine placement, samples six mine cells from the remaining locations, and applies the zero-cell opening. • A deterministic constraint solver must then be able to finish without guessing: it deduces safe cells from adjacent-number constraints and reveals the lexicographically first deduced-safe cell at each step. For the 8 turn training environments, we set a bound of [ 6 , 8 ] [6,8] turns to solve the puzzle and for the 12 turn environments, we set a limit of [ 6 , 12 ] [6,12] turns. • We further filter this set to select non-trivial boards by comparing two non-guessing policies. The naive policy uniformly samples among provably safe cells, whereas the heuristic policy prioritizes provably-safe cells that are likely to flood-fill adjacent zero-cell regions or unexplored areas. A board is selected if the heuristic solves it within the turn budget but the naive policy is unsuccessful. Using this procedure, we generate 9,500 9{,}500 training and 500 500 testing puzzles.

sections.heading: E.4 Model prompt and interaction format
sections.text: Each episode begins with a system message and a user message. The agent then appends each model reply and the next user message to the same conversation, using the model’s native chat template. The eight-turn training runs use the following system message verbatim; the per-turn response limit is 4,096 4{,}096 tokens. There are no example moves in the prompt. ⬇ You are playing Minesweeper on a 6 by 6 board that contains 6 mines . Your only valid action is reveal ( row , col ). The board is given as a Python list of lists named board , and board [ row ][ col ] is the cell you reveal with reveal ( row , col ). Indices start at 0: board [0] is the top row , board [5] is the bottom row , board [ row ][0] is the leftmost cell of a row , and board [ row ][5] is the rightmost . There is no row 6 and no column 6. A "#" entry is an unrevealed cell . An integer is the number of mines in its neighboring cells . The initial reveal has already been made and zero cells use normal flood fill . You have at most 8 turns to reveal every non - mine cell . Each turn you cannot spend more than 4096 tokens , reasoning included : a reply cut off at that limit loses the episode . Keep your reasoning brief . The last line of your reply must be exactly one action , in this format : reveal ( row , col ) Only that last line is read , so nothing may follow it . There are no second chances : a reply with no action on its final line or a cell outside the board loses the episode outright , exactly as revealing a mine would . Revealing a cell that is already visible does not lose the episode , but it uncovers nothing and still uses up one of your turns . The user message supplies the current board. For example, the first message for training seed 12438 12438 is: ⬇ Turns remaining : 8 board = [ ["#", "#", "#", "#", "#", "#"], ["#", 2, 1, 2, 3, "#"], ["#", 2, 0, 0, 1, 1], ["#", 2, 1, 1, 0, 0], ["#", "#", "#", 1, 0, 0], ["#", "#", "#", 1, 0, 0], ] You must uncover all the safe cells before time runs out . Answer with the 0- indexed row and column , so reveal ( row , col ) reveals board [ row ][ col ]; rows and columns each run from 0 to 5. Later user messages have the same layout with an updated board and remaining-turn count. If the model selects an already visible cell, the next user message also begins with the following notice, with the coordinates substituted for the attempted action: ⬇ Your action reveal (2, 3) named board [2][3], which was already revealed : nothing was uncovered and that turn is spent . Pick an unrevealed ("#") cell .

Learn more × Back to arXiv License: arXiv.org perpetual non-exclusive license arXiv:2610.20401v1 [cs.LG] 14 Oct 2026 Training Language Models to Fail Gracefully Thanks: Project website, code, and other assets: https://zanette-labs.github.io/failing-gracefully/ Daman Arora † † thanks: Correspondence: {damana,azanette}@andrew.cmu.edu Affiliation: Carnegie Mellon University Xuecheng Liu Affiliation: Carnegie Mellon University Himanshu Gaurav Singh Affiliation: UC Berkeley Fahim Tajwar Affiliation: Carnegie Mellon University Abitha Thankaraj Affiliation: Carnegie Mellon University Ruslan Salakhutdinov Affiliation: Carnegie Mellon University Haiwen Feng Affiliation: UC Berkeley Yuda Song Affiliation: Carnegie Mellon University Andrea Zanette Affiliation: Carnegie Mellon University Abstract Reinforcement learning makes language models better at solving tasks, but the same mechanism also rewards guessing. When success is the only way to earn reward, opting for a safe fallback is always worse than a long-shot attempt. When a wrong action can corrupt a database or ship broken code, that incentive can be costly. Therefore, we propose training models to fail gracefully : to preserve successful behavior whenever possible while learning to execute a safe fallback policy when acting would be unreliable. However, naively using policy gradients with intermediate reward for fallback behavior is brittle due to unfavorable optimization dynamics. We address this challenge with GracefulRL , which reshapes the optimization landscape to promote graceful failure. Importantly, this behavior emerges directly from outcome-level reward signals, without annotations specifying when to fall back or additional inference-time machinery such as a verifier. Across a range of tasks and scales, we train models that largely preserve their task-solving capability while selectively falling back when acting would be unreliable. More broadly, our results show that reinforcement learning can not only incentivize models to succeed, but also to reason about the limits of their capabilities and change course when they determine that success is out of reach. 1 Introduction Large Language Models (LLMs) can now complete in minutes tasks that would take a person hours. They write and refactor code across whole repositories, produce long mathematical arguments, and act as agents that edit files and run commands on our behalf. Significant improvements in such capabilities can be attributed to Reinforcement learning (RL) in domains with verifiable rewards such as coding and mathematics, ( Guo et al., 2025 ; OpenAI et al., 2026 ; Shao et al., 2024 ) where models are rewarded for successful task completion ( Lambert et al., 2025 ; Luo et al., 2025 ) . These improvements are often measured by metrics such as accuracy or success rate, but these metrics say little about how the model behaves when it does not succeed . Models are imperfectly informed and computationally bounded during inference. Therefore, there always exist situations in which appropriate actions cannot be reliably determined. In such cases, reinforcement learning can incentivize guessing, as a strategy to maximize reward ( Kalai et al., 2025 ) , laying the burden of verification on the user. Someone needs to check the proof, review the pull request, and confirm what the agent actually did. This verification can be tedious and prone to errors, and when it fails, mistakes can propagate into consequential actions. Therefore, we want models that change course when success is unlikely. If they can solve a task reliably, they should. If they cannot, they should do something else: revert their changes, inform the user that they are stuck, or hand the task to a different model. We call this behaviour failing gracefully . Not only does graceful failure avoid harmful actions, it also helps build trust with users. The naive way to train for this behavior is to reward success most, fallback second, and failure least. In principle, this should teach the model to keep trying when success is within reach and to fallback when it is not. Surprisingly, we find that learning this behavior with standard policy-gradient methods ( Williams, 1992 ) and their derivatives ( Shao et al., 2024 ) can be brittle. In the worst case, they can collapse to a model that always falls back and stops solving the task altogether (Section 3 ). We trace this failure to unfavorable optimization dynamics : the objective expresses the behavior we want, but the optimization process does not reliably produce it. We introduce GracefulRL , a reinforcement learning approach designed to avoid this pathology. We modify the optimization landscape which lets us maintain pressure to solve the task, while simultaneously encouraging the model to fall back rather than making an error when success is unlikely. Crucially, the model learns when to fall back from its own interaction with the environment with no labels specifying which problems are too hard, and no separate uncertainty model or post-hoc decision rule at inference time. Across navigation, mathematical reasoning, and multi-turn Minesweeper, GracefulRL learns selective fallback while preserving strong task performance. On AIME, it reduces the error rate from 79.1% to 8.9% while sacrificing only 3.1 percentage points of success relative to standard RL. In Minesweeper, it improves both sides of the tradeoff, increasing success while reducing errors. Perhaps most strikingly, we find that the model verbalizes its decision making strategy in its chain-of-thought when its about to change course. Overall, our results suggest that reinforcement learning can not only improve a model’s task performance, but also shape it’s behavior when success is unlikely. Figure 1: Learning to fail gracefully. Vanishing gradients in policy gradients are well known, studied even in tabular MDPs ( Agarwal et al., 2021 ) . Mei et al. (2020) identify a “gravity well” induced by the softmax parameterization, leading to poor optimization while Li et al. (2021) further show that softmax PG methods can require exponentially many steps to converge. More recently, Razin et al. (2024) studied vanishing gradients in LLM RL finetuning showing that the gradient becomes small when the reward variance of the policy is small. Our analysis complements these results by studying a specific case with 3 outcomes where standard PG methods can get trapped near saturated outcomes. We further show that the GracefulRL objective avoids this pathology, retaining a non-vanishing optimization signal near such saturated solutions. Likelihood-based objectives for RL. Recent work has explored replacing expected-reward objectives with likelihood-based objectives exemplified by MaxRL ( Tajwar et al., 2026 ) and TailRL ( Ramasubramanian et al., 2026 ) . They show that these objectives admit an interpretation as a harmonically weighted combination of Best ​ @ ⁡ k \operatorname{Best@}k objectives. We arrive at the same solution through an optimization perspective. We analyse how the logarithmic objective avoids gradient suppression near undesirable saturation which prevents a failure mode in expected reward maximization. Uncertainty quantification for LLMs. Selective classification studies the tradeoff between prediction risk and coverage ( Chow, 1970 ; El-Yaniv and Wiener, 2010 ; Geifman and El-Yaniv, 2019 ; Liu et al., 2019 ) . Recent work on LLM uncertainty and abstention has constructed specialized data to train refusal behavior ( Zhang et al., 2024 ; Zhao et al., 2026 ) , elicited verbalized confidence ( Kadavath et al., 2022 ; Lin et al., 2022 ; Tian et al., 2023 ; Xiong et al., 2024 ) , estimated uncertainty through repeated sampling ( Manakul et al., 2023 ; Kang et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2023 ) , combined multiple models at inference time ( Stengel-Eskin et al., 2024 ) , directly trained models for uncertainty quantification ( Damani et al., 2026 ; Leng et al., 2025 ; Chandak et al., 2026 ) , or introduced inference-time stopping rules that detect when continued reasoning is unlikely to help ( Davidov et al., 2026 ) . Our goal however is different: rather than estimating uncertainty, we aim to learn how the policy should act under uncertainty . This distinction becomes important in sequential decision-making settings, where uncertainty quantification is not enough: the fallback policy execution must also be a part of the policy itself and its learnt end-to-end. Moreover, our approach doesn’t require specialized datasets, is not LLM-specific, and naturally extends to multi-step interactions. Learning abstention with RL. Some prior works try to use RL for abstention. For instance, Xu et al. (2024) use knowledge feedback to identify questions outside a model’s knowledge boundary and reward rejection on these examples. Wei et al. (2026) , Pan et al. (2026) , Ma et al. (2026) , Wu et al. (2026) and Zhai et al. (2026) directly train for abstention using policy gradient style methods such as GRPO and PPO with and without heuristics such as reward tuning or modifying advantages. However, we show that this procedure can be brittle depending on the model and the task. We show that our approach is more robust and avoids issues associated with PG methods in a principled manner. Moreover, our formulation treats fallback as a general behavior rather than an LLM-specific refusal, allowing it to extend to sequential and non-language decision-making settings. Safe and constrained reinforcement learning. Our work is also related to safe RL, which studies improving task performance while satisfying safety requirements or constraints ( García and Fernández, 2015 ; Achiam et al., 2017 ) . Other approaches intervene when an unsafe action is likely; for example, Recovery RL learns a separate recovery policy that takes control near constraint-violating regions ( Thananjeyan et al., 2021 ) . In contrast, we jointly learn task success and graceful fallback, without a secondary recovery policy intervening. 7 Conclusion and Limitations We formulated graceful failure as an RL problem in which an agent must learn when to pursue task success and when to fall back safely. We showed that naively optimizing the expected reward can be brittle due to the underlying optimization dynamics.
